article.overview: A robotic crane is a lightweight, deployable manipulator intended to unload, lift and position heavy payloads on the lunar surface, typically from a lander's deck. Unlike a serial robotic arm, which carries loads mainly as bending moments, the NASA Lightweight Surface Manipulation System (LSMS) concept uses a structurally efficient truss frame with cable actuation, so that its members are loaded mainly in tension and compression. NASA states that this gives higher mechanical advantage, meaning greater payload mass at a given reach, and a lower system mass [1][2]. The concepts in the sources reviewed are engineering prototypes, breadboards and proposals. None is documented as having flown to the Moon [1][2][5][6].
article.description: A robotic crane for surface use combines two functions. It is a crane, which suspends and moves a load on cables, and it is a manipulator, which can grasp a payload at its tip and position it precisely. The 2008 NASA description of the LSMS calls it a versatile lifting device that works both as a cable-suspended crane and as a manipulator, with a tool at the tip that rigidly grasps the payload for precise positioning [1]. NASA Langley later described the system as moving like a human arm while reaching farther, with swappable tools [3]. The European concepts follow a similar pattern. ESA's Loader is a folding long-arm crane with two grippers [5]. ESA's MANUS is a robotic arm for cargo handling, rover power transfer and regolith scooping [6]. The term robotic crane therefore covers a family of designs in which the balance between crane and manipulator functions differs.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a robotic crane on the Moon is to move heavy cargo from a landed vehicle to the surface, or to a mobility asset, without relying on astronauts to carry each item. NASA states that Artemis landers need a viable payload offload device for large cargo, and that commercial landers need offloading and added capabilities [2]. NASA's concept goals for the LSMS are a manipulator for payloads of very different sizes and masses that is lightweight, power-efficient and has a small footprint on the lander [2][3]. NASA's 2020 slide set lists concept functions including precision payload lifting and unloading, deploying structures, outpost setup, inspection, site survey and mapping, regolith excavation and handling, 3D printing, and connections and e-beam welding [2]. These are design intentions, not demonstrated capabilities. The European concepts focus on cargo offloading and deployment. The Loader is intended to lift cargo off an Argonaut-class lander and place it up to six metres away [5]. MANUS is intended to load and unload cargo, hand items to rovers or astronauts, act as a rover power connector and scoop regolith [6].
article.operating_principle: A cable-supported crane carries its load on a set of cables, so its behaviour depends on cable geometry and tension rather than on the stiffness of a rigid arm. The LSMS truss frame is cable-actuated [3]. The 2020 NASA concept targets self-levelling of up to plus or minus 15 degrees and self-deployment [2]. A heavy payload suspended on a single lift point can swing or rotate, because the lifting force is not aligned with its weight. NASA Langley's ARPHOLS work addresses this with two motor-driven capstans that change the lengths of a cable routed to three or four attachment points on the payload, which controls its orientation during a lift [4]. The prototype described in that paper was built from a LEGO Technic set and tested off-site because of COVID-19 restrictions. The initial testing used manual control, and the paper presents the algorithms needed for full automation [4]. The 2008 paper lists teleoperated or automated operation as a design requirement, but publishes no performance data for it [1]. The Loader has a passive, spring-loaded gripper that locks without power and a battery-powered gripper for fine positioning [5].
article.scientific_importance: NASA's 2020 overview states that Artemis landers require a viable payload offload device for large cargo, and that long-reach, high-mass payload handling for Moon and Mars surfaces did not exist at that time [2]. It notes that planetary-surface serial manipulators do not scale to heavy payloads. The Mars InSight lander's 1.8 m arm offloaded a 29 kg seismometer about 1 m onto the Martian surface, a single time [2]. A scalable crane-type manipulator could let different lander designs offload heavy cargo, reduce the need for purpose-built hardware, and support later tasks such as inspection, regolith handling and construction [2][3]. Its importance is therefore largely enabling. It would make other surface payloads practical to deliver and place. That value is a projection, and none of the crane concepts is documented as having performed a lunar offload.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a robotic crane. The examples below range from a 2008 ground prototype to 2026 breadboard and demonstrator hardware and to a 2020 proposal. Their key values describe different concepts and are not directly comparable.

examples.name: NASA Lightweight Surface Manipulation System (LSMS)
examples.type: Lunar manipulator and crane; ground-tested prototypes and a proposed proto-flight unit
examples.status: Prototype and development hardware. No lunar flight is reported in the sources reviewed.
key_figures: Field-tested prototype: 1000 kg tip capacity, 2008, Moses Lake, WA (measured load not published) [1][2]
Composite variant mass: estimated below 3% of maximum lunar tip payload (design estimate) [1]
Full-size payload goal: around one metric ton; reach about 25 ft (goal) [3]
Mini-LSMS reach: about six feet (about 1.8 m) [3]
examples.description: The LSMS is a lightweight robotic crane built around a structurally efficient truss frame with cable actuation. It is designed to offload payloads from a lander and to function as a manipulator [1][3]. A 1000 kg tip-capacity LSMS prototype was field tested at Moses Lake, Washington in 2008 [1][2]. The lifted load and detailed test data are not published in the sources read. The 2008 paper estimates that a future high-performance composite variant would have a mass below 3 per cent of the maximum lunar payload lifted at the tip. This is a design estimate, not a measurement [1]. The 2020 NASA overview lists a 500 kg LSMS mass goal, self-levelling of plus or minus 15 degrees, self-deployment, and a three-year, $22 million Phase I programme to a proto-flight unit at TRL 4 to 6 [2]. It also lists a 5,000 kg tip-capable HLS-class engineering demonstration unit and proto-flight unit as deliverables [2]. NASA's 2021 article describes the new full-size version as designed for payloads of around one metric ton (about 2,200 lb), with about a 25 ft (about 7.6 m) reach. It describes a mini-LSMS with about a six-foot (about 1.8 m) reach for smaller CLPS landers. It states that proto-flight hardware was built and tested under the current project, without publishing metrics [3].

examples.name: ESA and COMOTI/Initium 'Loader' lunar cargo crane
examples.type: Lunar cargo crane; scaled demonstrator tested on Earth
examples.status: Demonstrator. The developers state that much work remains to refine the crane.
key_figures: Design target: up to 1000 kg lifted, placed up to 6 m from the lander [5]
Scaled model: 30 kg lifted in Earth gravity; ESA equates this to a little over 180 kg on the Moon [5]
Total mass and power: not stated [5]
examples.description: The Loader is a lunar cargo crane developed by the Romanian research institute COMOTI with Initium Space, under ESA's Technology Development Element [5]. The design target is to lift up to 1000 kg of cargo off a lander such as Argonaut and place it up to six metres away [5]. The crane launches folded on the lander's payload deck and unfolds on the surface. A cable-management system and a defined unfolding sequence keep it compact in the stowed configuration. A levelling system keeps it vertical on sloped terrain. A long two-joint arm ends in a passive, spring-loaded gripper that locks without power and a battery-powered gripper for fine positioning [5]. A scaled model was tested at ESA's Planetary Robotics Laboratory in the Netherlands. It lifted 30 kg under Earth gravity, which ESA equates to a little over 180 kg on the Moon. This is a gravity-scaling statement, not a lunar test. ESA says the full-size crane will be more than twice as large [5]. The total mass and power of the Loader are not stated [5].

examples.name: Redwire MANUS lunar robotic manipulator (ESA-supported)
examples.status: Breadboard model delivered to ESA in May 2026. This is development hardware, not flight hardware.
key_figures: MANUS mass, reach and payload: not published [6]
Argonaut delivery capability as stated in the MANUS release: 1,500 to 1,800 kg (lander figure) [6]
examples.description: Redwire delivered a MANUS Breadboard Model to ESA, announced on 21 May 2026. Testing covered the arm and a tool-changer [6]. The reported scenarios were payload handling, end-effector actuation with wireless data and power transfer, range-extender manipulation and automatic deployment. The release describes these as successful and reports strong joint-space accuracy [6]. The intended functions are to load and unload cargo from ESA's Argonaut lander, hand cargo to a rover, the lunar surface or an astronaut, act as a rover power connector, and scoop lunar regolith [6]. No mass, reach or payload figures are published for MANUS. The 1,500 to 1,800 kg figure in the release refers to what Argonaut will deliver, not to MANUS [6].

examples.name: ARPHOLS auto-rigging payload orientation prototype (NASA Langley and Marshall)
examples.type: Payload rigging and orientation control concept; not a crane arm
examples.status: Laboratory-scale prototype. Initial testing used manual control.
key_figures: Prototype scale: LEGO Technic laboratory model [4]
Test mode: manual control for initial tests; automation algorithms presented [4]
examples.description: ARPHOLS uses two motorised capstans that adjust the lengths of a single cable routed through pulleys and attached to three or four points on the payload. Rotating the capstans changes the orientation of the suspended payload [4]. The prototype was built from a LEGO Technic set and tested off-site because of COVID-19 restrictions. Its motors were controlled sequentially over Bluetooth [4]. The paper's stated aim is a fully automated system that senses the deck incline, adjusts the rigging, lifts and moves the payload stably, and offloads it. The paper presents the algorithms, but the initial testing reported used manual control [4].

examples.name: High-capacity ATHLETE offloader concept (JPL)
examples.type: Related multi-limbed mobility and manipulation concept; not a dedicated crane
examples.status: Concept preprint. No hardware reported in the text read.
key_figures: Stepped payload capacities and vehicle masses: stated in the full paper, not retrieved [7]
examples.description: The concept proposes an Artemis-class ATHLETE, a multi-limbed robotic platform for surface traverse, precise placement and offloading of heavy habitats from high-decked landers. Each limb can work as a single crane [7]. The abstract states that the paper gives vehicle masses for stepped payload capacities in Earth, Mars and lunar gravity, but these figures were not available in the text read, so none is reported here [7].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Overall dimensions are not stated in the sources reviewed for the 2008 LSMS prototype, the Loader or MANUS. Reach figures are available. NASA Langley gives about 25 ft (about 7.6 m) for the full-size LSMS version and about 6 ft (about 1.8 m) for the mini-LSMS [3]. The 2020 slide concept carries 4 m labels whose meaning is not explained in the text extracted [2]. The Loader reaches up to six metres from the lander [5]. Its full-size version is described as more than twice the size of the scaled model [5].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No measured mass for a robotic crane is published in the sources reviewed. The 2020 NASA overview gives an LSMS mass goal of 500 kg [2]. This is a design target for the system, not an achieved value. The 2008 paper estimates that a future high-performance composite variant would have a mass below 3 per cent of the maximum lunar payload lifted at the tip. The paper labels this a design estimate for future development, not a measurement [1]. The Loader's total mass is not stated [5], and the MANUS breadboard's mass is not stated [6].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power requirements are not publicly specified for any of the examples. The 2020 NASA proposal describes the concept as lightweight and power-efficient, with only basic motor control and sensor output in scope for the proto-flight unit [2]. The Loader's battery powers its fine-positioning gripper, but battery capacity and total power are not stated [5]. The MANUS breadboard is described as supporting wireless power and data transfer to end-effectors and rovers, without figures [6].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The sources reviewed do not publish environmental test specifications for thermal, vacuum, radiation or dust exposure for the LSMS, Loader or MANUS. Some operating context is available. Lunar landers are designed to land safely on slopes of up to 15 degrees [4]. The 2020 NASA proposal planned full-scale vibration testing at Goddard Space Flight Center and environmental tests of the primary mechanisms and cables [2]. General lunar-surface conditions, including vacuum, extreme thermal cycling and abrasive regolith dust, are background knowledge rather than findings from these sources. They would apply to any surface mechanism. Dust, thermal control and cable durability therefore remain open engineering questions for any crane design.
article.limitations: The crane concepts are not interchangeable. A 1000 kg tip-capacity prototype, a 500 kg system mass goal, a 1000 kg Loader target and a breadboard MANUS arm each describe different things, and they should not be compared as like-for-like results. Heavy cable-supported lifts also need active control of swing and orientation, which the ARPHOLS work addresses but has demonstrated only with a laboratory-scale prototype under manual control [4]. Reach and payload capacity grow the structural, stowage and deployment challenges. The LSMS overview itself states that the system must be integrated with a lander, and that integration has not been reported as complete [2][3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A robotic crane is normally a lander-mounted or lander-deployed system. It must be stowed compactly on the lander deck, unfold and level itself on the surface, and then offload cargo. The sources describe two main roles: offloading heavy cargo from a lander, and moving or placing payloads on the surface [1][2][3][5].
transportation_process: Integrate the folded crane onto the lander's payload deck. The Loader concept is described as launching folded on the deck, with a cable-management system to keep it compact [5].
Launch the lander on a launch vehicle. The sources reviewed do not specify the launch vehicle for any crane concept.
Transfer the lander to the Moon and land it. The ARPHOLS discussion notes landers designed for slopes of up to 15 degrees, so the crane must cope with a tilted deck [4].
Deploy the crane on the surface and level it. The LSMS 2020 target is self-levelling of up to plus or minus 15 degrees [2]. The Loader includes a levelling system for sloped terrain [5].
Lift and place payloads, controlling orientation and swing during the lift [4].

Connect power and data where needed. MANUS is described as providing wireless power and data transfer to end-effectors and rovers [6]. Lander power and communications integration for LSMS was listed as a follow-on task [2].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment methods in the sources reviewed are concept-specific. The LSMS concept is designed for self-deployment from stowage [2], and NASA's 2020 slides show deployment from vertical stowage and offloading from a mobility asset [2]. The Loader is designed to unfold from a folded launch configuration on the lander's payload deck [5]. The MANUS breadboard testing reported automatic deployment as one successful scenario [6]. No robotic crane in this class is documented in the sources as having deployed on the Moon.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: In 2008, the first-generation LSMS, a 1000 kg tip-capacity lunar prototype, completed field trials at Moses Lake, Washington. These trials were a ground analogue test, not a lunar mission [1][2]. The Mars InSight arm, a 1.8 m arm, offloaded a 29 kg seismometer on Mars, once [2]. Neither example is a lunar crane flight. The 2021 NASA article describes the Langley work as preparing a flight-like proto-flight version, with no test metrics given [3]. ARPHOLS, a NASA Langley and Marshall paper with a publication date not confirmed from the text read, reports a LEGO-built orientation-control prototype [4].The high-capacity ATHLETE concept is a related multi-limbed offloader, not a dedicated crane [7].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No robotic crane described here has been verified against a specific lander interface. NASA's 2020 overview names the target as a large commercial lander for the proto-flight demonstration, and a follow-on phase to integrate with a commercial or NASA lunar lander [2]. A 2021 NASA article mentions CLPS landers as the intended users of the mini-LSMS [3]. These are intentions, not verified compatibility. ESA's Loader is designed to fly on Argonaut landers that carry up to 1,500 kg of cargo [5]. The MANUS breadboard is developed for Argonaut, which ESA's MANUS source states will deliver 1,500 to 1,800 kg to the surface [6]. The two ESA-related sources give different Argonaut figures. Compatibility with any named lander would need the lander's mass, mounting, landing-load, power and data interfaces, which are not published in the sources reviewed.

article.historical_significance: The NASA LSMS line dates from around 2008. The 2008 AIAA paper reports that a first-generation test-bed completed field tests at Moses Lake, Washington [1]. The work then continued through NASA's Game Changing Development programme and the Lunar Surface Innovation Initiative [2][3]. Commercial and international interest has followed. NASA gave a 2020 overview for Blue Origin [2]. ESA's Loader and MANUS programmes in 2026 show European interest in lunar cargo cranes and manipulators [5][6]. None has been reported in these sources as having flown to the Moon.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The NASA LSMS figures come from different documents and dates. The 2008 field test shows the prototype was built and tested, but the lifted load and test data are not published in the sources read [1]. The 2020 NASA overview gives targets, and the 2021 article says proto-flight hardware was built and tested, without metrics [2][3]. The page's last-updated date is 2026, but its text describes no later progress, so the current status of the LSMS is uncertain [3]. The Loader figures are design targets. The 30 kg scaled model was tested under Earth gravity, and its Moon equivalence is a gravity-scaling statement made in the ESA article, not a lunar test [5]. The MANUS breadboard has no published mass, reach or payload figures [6]. The 2020 NASA slide labels for 5,000 kg and 10,000 kg are not clearly assigned in the text extracted, so they are not relied on here [2]. The Argonaut payload figure differs between ESA-related sources, 1,500 kg and 1,500 to 1,800 kg [5][6]. The ATHLETE paper was read only as an abstract, so its stepped mass figures are not reported [7]. ARPHOLS is a laboratory-scale LEGO prototype with manual initial testing, and its publication date is not confirmed from the text read [4].

data_quality_notes: Lunar crane concepts are not interchangeable: the 2008 LSMS prototype, the 2020 LSMS targets, the ESA Loader target, the MANUS breadboard and the ARPHOLS laboratory prototype describe different things.
The 2008 LSMS field test (Moses Lake, WA) is documented as completed, but the lifted load and test data were not published in the sources read.

The 2020 NASA overview gives a 500 kg system mass goal, a 5,000 kg tip-capable engineering demonstration target and a 10,000 kg slide label; the 10,000 kg label is not clearly assigned in the text extracted and is not relied on.
The NASA 2021 article's page was last updated in June 2026, but its text describes no progress after proto-flight build and test. Current LSMS status is uncertain.
The Loader's Moon equivalence (30 kg Earth-gravity lift to a little over 180 kg on the Moon) is an ESA gravity-scaling statement, not a lunar test.
Argonaut delivery capability is 1,500 kg in the ESA Loader source and 1,500 to 1,800 kg in the Redwire MANUS release. The two sources differ and no compatibility is asserted.
The NASA LSMS image caption is partial: only its opening sentence was retrieved.
The ESA image shows the Planetary Robotics Lab test area per its accessibility description; the source does not confirm that a crane is visible in it.
The ARPHOLS publication date is not confirmed from the text read. The NTRS identifier suggests 2024.
The ATHLETE concept was read from its abstract only; its stepped mass figures were not retrieved.
A secondary search summary reported joystick teleoperation for a later LSMS demonstration. This was not verified in a primary source and is not included.
Fetched page text in one source contained instructions aimed at the tooling. These were ignored and are not part of the article.
